To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1. The ability to learn to form perceptually salient groups is limited by the type and amount of connectivity available in a network; 2. Bottom-up connections are insufficient to learn to form groups in complex scenes; 3. Horizontal connections are necessary to support incremental grouping; 4. Top-down connections are necessary

(1) increasing the difficulty of a perceptual grouping task strains the performance of networks that rely only on bottom-up connections; (2) horizontal connections resolve this straining by supporting incremental grouping of objects; and (3) top-down connections rescue performance on a task with high-level object grouping cues by modifying coarse object predictions.
(a) horizontal connections support incremental grouping, and (b) top-down connections support object individuation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how the brain learns to form perceptual groupings.
understanding the neural mechanisms that support visual grouping and object individuation in visual scenes.
the computational role of different types of neural connectivity for perceptual grouping.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our results suggest that the brain uses a combination of horizontal and top-down interactions, in addition to bottom-up connections, to form perceptual grouping.
the neural network architectures featuring all the interactions can learn to form perceptually groups more flexibly.

the relative contributions of bottom-up, top-down and horizontal connections to perceptual groupings depends on the type of visual cues that are used for perceptual groupings, and that a model featuring all these connections is better suited for learning to form perceptual groupings than a model relying on a single connection type.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the neural mechanisms for perceptually grouping objects in visual scenes arise from interactions between bottom-up, horizontal (lateral) and top-down connectivity in a neural network.
the combination of bottom-up, bottom-up, and top-down connectivity in the brain enables flexible perceptual grouping.
the neural mechanisms for perceptually grouping objects can be understood as an interplay between bottom-up, horizontal (lateral) and top-down connections in the brain.
The main takeaway from our work is that
bottom-up connectivity alone is insufficient to learn to form perceptural groups in complex scenes, and that horizontal and top-down connections play complementary roles.
the brain's visual system is likely to use all three types of connections to flexibly learn to perceive visual objects.
the brain likely uses all of these interactions in parallel to form perceptual groupings.
